questions.stem: A 28-year-old physiologist is studying the principal extracellular buffer system. Which buffer system is most important for buffering acid loads in plasma?
explanations: Incorrect. Phosphate buffering is significant intracellularly and in urine but minor in plasma.
Incorrect. Hemoglobin is important in red cells but is intracellular.

Correct. The bicarbonate/CO2 system is the principal ECF buffer. Henderson-Hasselbalch: pH = 6.1 + log([HCO3−] / 0.03 × PCO2). The system is 'open' — CO2 is exhaled by lungs and HCO3− is regulated by kidneys, allowing rapid and effective buffering.
Incorrect. Albumin is a smaller plasma buffer.
Incorrect. Bone is important for chronic acid loads but slow.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old researcher studies bicarbonate reabsorption. Which nephron segment reabsorbs the LARGEST fraction of filtered HCO3−?
explanations: Correct. The PCT reabsorbs ~80% of filtered HCO3−, principally via apical NHE3 (Na+/H+ exchanger): H+ secreted into the lumen combines with HCO3− to form H2CO3, which is dehydrated by luminal carbonic anhydrase IV to CO2 + H2O. CO2 enters the cell, where intracellular CA II re-forms H+ and HCO3−; HCO3− exits basolaterally via NBCe1.
Incorrect. TAL reabsorbs ~10–15%.
Incorrect. DCT contributes minimally.
Incorrect. CCD has further H+ secretion / HCO3− adjustment but much smaller volumes.
Incorrect. MCD adjusts urine pH at the end stage.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old researcher studies the proximal tubule. Which apical transporter is principally responsible for H+ secretion in the PCT?
explanations: Incorrect. NKCC2 is in the TAL.
Incorrect. NCC is in the DCT.

Correct. NHE3 (Na+/H+ exchanger isoform 3) is the apical PCT transporter that secretes H+ in exchange for Na+. The H+ combines with luminal HCO3− to be effectively reabsorbed. NHE3 also operates in the TAL and contributes there. Inhibited by angiotensin II (stimulates) — explained PT bicarbonate handling regulation.
Incorrect. ENaC is in the collecting duct.
Incorrect. H+/K+-ATPase is in α-intercalated cells of the collecting duct.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old researcher studies carbonic anhydrase isoforms. Which isoform is membrane-bound at the brush border of proximal tubular cells?
explanations: Incorrect. CA I is principally in red blood cells.
Incorrect. CA II is cytoplasmic (intracellular in PT and many other tissues).

Correct. Carbonic anhydrase IV is the brush-border / luminal isoform of the proximal tubule. It catalyzes the dehydration of luminal H2CO3 to CO2 + H2O, enabling efficient HCO3− reabsorption. CA II (intracellular) then re-forms H+ and HCO3−. Acetazolamide inhibits both isoforms.
Incorrect. CA IX is associated with cancer biology.
Incorrect. CA XII is in distal nephron / various tissues.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man is given oral acetazolamide for high-altitude sickness. Within hours, urine pH rises from 5.5 to 7.5 and HCO3− level falls. Which mechanism best explains the effect?
explanations: Incorrect. Acetazolamide does not act at ENaC.

Correct. Acetazolamide inhibits carbonic anhydrase (II and IV) in the proximal tubule, reducing H+ secretion and impairing HCO3− reabsorption. Result: bicarbonaturia, alkaline urine, mild metabolic acidosis. Used: glaucoma (reduces aqueous humor production), altitude sickness (induces metabolic acidosis offsetting respiratory alkalosis), idiopathic intracranial hypertension, and as a weak diuretic. Adverse: alkaline urine promotes Ca-phosphate stones; sulfa allergy potential; metabolic acidosis with chronic use.
Incorrect. Acetazolamide does not inhibit NKCC2.
Incorrect. Acetazolamide does not directly inhibit H+-ATPase.
Incorrect. Acetazolamide is not an aldosterone antagonist.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old researcher studies the cellular structure of the distal collecting duct. Which cell type is responsible for H+ secretion?
explanations: Incorrect. Principal cells handle Na+ (ENaC) and K+ (ROMK), not H+.

Correct. α-intercalated cells secrete H+ via apical H+-ATPase (and H+/K+-ATPase). H+ combines with urinary buffers (NH3 → NH4+; HPO4²− → H2PO4−) for excretion. Basolateral AE1 (Cl−/HCO3− exchanger) returns HCO3− to plasma, generating 'new' HCO3−. Aldosterone enhances α-intercalated H+ secretion via the lumen-negative voltage created by ENaC-driven Na+ reabsorption.
Incorrect. β-intercalated cells SECRETE HCO3− (do the reverse) via apical pendrin and basolateral H+-ATPase.
Incorrect. Macula densa cells are part of the JGA.
Incorrect. Mesangial cells are in the glomerulus.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old researcher studies the β-intercalated cell. Which is the principal apical transporter?
explanations: Incorrect. The α-intercalated cell has apical H+-ATPase.

Correct. β-intercalated cells secrete HCO3− into the lumen via apical pendrin (Cl−/HCO3− exchanger, SLC26A4) and reabsorb H+ basolaterally via H+-ATPase. They function in alkalosis to excrete excess HCO3−. Pendrin mutations cause Pendred syndrome (sensorineural hearing loss + thyroid goiter).
Incorrect. ENaC is in principal cells.
Incorrect. NHE3 is proximal.
Incorrect. AQP2 is the ADH-regulated water channel in principal cells.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old physiologist studies renal ammoniagenesis. Which substrate is principally metabolized in the proximal tubule to generate NH4+?
explanations: Incorrect. Glycine is not the principal substrate.

Correct. Glutamine is the principal substrate for renal ammoniagenesis. PCT cells take up glutamine and metabolize it via glutaminase and glutamate dehydrogenase to α-ketoglutarate + 2 NH4+. NH4+ is secreted into the tubular fluid (via NHE3 with NH4+ substituting for H+), trapped in the medulla, and excreted in urine. Each NH4+ excreted represents 'new' HCO3− added to plasma. Acidosis upregulates ammoniagenesis (chronic adaptation).
Incorrect. Urea is the breakdown product, not the substrate.
Incorrect. Glucose is not the principal substrate.
Incorrect. Lactate is not the principal substrate.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old researcher studies how NH4+ is concentrated in the medulla. NH4+ is reabsorbed in the TAL by which transporter, where it substitutes for K+?
explanations: Incorrect. ENaC is in the collecting duct.
Incorrect. ROMK recycles K+ apically in the TAL.

Correct. NH4+ substitutes for K+ at NKCC2 in the TAL, allowing apical reabsorption of NH4+ from tubular fluid into the medullary interstitium. This concentrates NH4+ in the medulla, where it is then secreted again into the late distal nephron. The NH4+ recycling supports a high medullary NH3/NH4+ gradient, allowing efficient titration of distal H+ secretion.
Incorrect. NCC is the DCT thiazide target.
Incorrect. NHE3 is in PCT and TAL but does not principally recycle NH4+ in TAL.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old researcher studies the principal urinary buffers. Which compound, in addition to NH4+, is the most important titratable acid buffer in the urine?
explanations: Incorrect. Sulfate is excreted but is not principally a buffer.

Correct. Phosphate (HPO4²−) is the principal urinary titratable acid buffer. As distal H+ is secreted, HPO4²− picks up H+ to become H2PO4−, allowing excretion as a 'titratable acid'. Total net acid excretion = NH4+ excretion + titratable acid (mostly H2PO4−) − HCO3− loss. Daily net acid excretion ~70 mEq/day matches dietary acid load on a typical Western diet.
Incorrect. Citrate is excreted but as conjugate base; not a titratable acid in the standard sense.
Incorrect. Albumin is largely retained, not excreted.
Incorrect. Lactate is metabolized.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old physiologist measures net acid excretion. Which formula correctly captures it?
explanations: Correct. Net acid excretion = (urinary NH4+) + (urinary titratable acid, mostly H2PO4−) − (urinary HCO3− loss). Approximately 70 mEq/day on a typical Western diet, balancing the metabolic acid load. NH4+ excretion is the principal mechanism for handling chronic acid loads (upregulates over days). Acidosis: ↑NH4+ excretion (compensation). RTA: inappropriately ↓ NH4+ excretion or ↓ titratable acid.
Incorrect. This formula is unrelated to acid excretion.
Incorrect. Volume × Na+ is sodium excretion.
Incorrect. K+ alone is not net acid.
Incorrect. Serum HCO3− is the concentration, not the rate of acid excretion.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with diarrhea has K+ 3.0, HCO3− 16, and a non-anion-gap metabolic acidosis. Urine pH is 5.0. Urine anion gap (Na+ + K+ − Cl−) is −20 (negative). Which best explains this pattern?
explanations: Incorrect. Distal RTA features high urine pH (>5.5) and POSITIVE urine anion gap (low NH4+).
Incorrect. Proximal RTA also typically features positive UAG.
Incorrect. Type 4 RTA features hyperkalemia.

Correct. Negative urine anion gap indicates HIGH urinary NH4+ excretion (Cl− > Na+ + K+ because Cl− accompanies the unmeasured NH4+ cation). This is the appropriate renal response to extra-renal acidosis (e.g., diarrhea). Distinguishes diarrhea from RTA (which has positive UAG = low NH4+, the renal lesion).
Incorrect. Bartter has alkalosis.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with a non-anion-gap metabolic acidosis has urine pH 6.5 (inappropriately high), urine anion gap +18 (positive), and K+ 3.0. Which best explains this pattern?
explanations: Incorrect. Diarrhea has negative UAG.

Correct. Type 1 (distal) RTA — failure of α-intercalated cell H+ secretion. Hallmarks: inability to acidify urine (urine pH >5.5 despite systemic acidosis), POSITIVE urine anion gap (low NH4+), HYPOkalemia. Causes: Sjögren syndrome, autoimmune, amphotericin B, lithium, hereditary. Treatment: oral alkali (potassium citrate, sodium bicarbonate), correct hypokalemia, address underlying cause.
Incorrect. Salicylate poisoning produces high anion-gap acidosis.
Incorrect. Adrenal insufficiency typically has hyperkalemic acidosis (type 4 pattern).
Incorrect. Lactic acidosis is high anion-gap.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman with distal RTA (urine pH 6.5, K+ 2.8, HCO3− 14) is being treated. Which oral therapy is most appropriate?
explanations: Incorrect. NaCl does not address the acid-base or K+ deficit.

Correct. Potassium citrate (or potassium bicarbonate, or sodium bicarbonate with K+ replacement) is the standard oral therapy for distal RTA. Citrate is metabolized to bicarbonate, correcting the acidosis AND supplying needed K+. Reduces stone formation in distal RTA (which predisposes to Ca-phosphate stones).
Incorrect. Furosemide worsens K+ wasting.
Incorrect. Acetazolamide WORSENS acidosis (it is a CA inhibitor).
Incorrect. Spironolactone may help with hyperkalemic states but is not first-line for distal RTA.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man with multiple myeloma has Fanconi syndrome with proximal RTA. Bicarbonate replacement requires very high doses to maintain serum HCO3− because urinary HCO3− losses are large. Which best characterizes proximal RTA?
choices: Defective proximal HCO3− reabsorption with reset threshold
Inability to lower urine pH at any HCO3−
explanations: Incorrect. Distal H+ defect is type 1, not type 2.

Correct. Proximal RTA — defective HCO3− reabsorption in PCT (lowered renal threshold for HCO3−). Once serum HCO3− falls below the new threshold, the kidney CAN acidify urine appropriately. Hallmarks: hypokalemia, often Fanconi syndrome (glycosuria, phosphaturia, aminoaciduria), urine pH that CAN be acidic when serum HCO3− is low. Causes: multiple myeloma (light chain proximal tubulopathy), Wilson disease, tenofovir, ifosfamide, cystinosis, heavy metals. Treatment: VERY high-dose alkali (alkali wastes in urine until threshold restored).
Incorrect. Type 4 RTA is hyperkalemic.
Incorrect. Distal acidification is preserved in proximal RTA.
Incorrect. Type 4 is the aldosterone-deficient pattern.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and CKD has K+ 5.6, HCO3− 18, and a non-anion-gap metabolic acidosis. Urine anion gap is positive. Renin and aldosterone are LOW. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
explanations: Incorrect. Type 1 RTA has hypokalemia.
Incorrect. Type 2 RTA has hypokalemia.

Correct. Type 4 RTA (hyperkalemic distal RTA) — typically from hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism in diabetic nephropathy. Mild non-anion-gap acidosis with HYPERkalemia. Reduced aldosterone effect lowers ENaC-driven Na+ reabsorption → reduced lumen-negative voltage → reduced K+ AND H+ secretion. Drug-induced type 4 also common (ACEi/ARB, K+-sparing diuretics, NSAIDs, heparin, trimethoprim, calcineurin inhibitors). Treatment: low-K+ diet, loop diuretic, fludrocortisone in selected cases.
Incorrect. Bartter has hypokalemic alkalosis.
Incorrect. Liddle has hypokalemic alkalosis with HTN.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with chronic salicylate ingestion has a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis with respiratory alkalosis. He has tinnitus, hyperthermia, and altered mental status. Which best explains the dual acid-base disturbance?
choices: Anion-gap acidosis plus direct respiratory stimulation
explanations: Incorrect. Salicylate is not principally a proximal RTA cause.

Correct. Salicylate (aspirin) overdose produces a CLASSIC mixed acid-base disorder: (1) high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis from accumulation of salicylate and other organic anions, plus uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation generating lactate; (2) primary respiratory alkalosis from direct stimulation of the medullary respiratory center. Other features: tinnitus, hyperthermia, AMS, hypoglycemia. Treatment: urinary alkalinization with sodium bicarbonate (ion-trapping increases excretion); hemodialysis for severe.
Incorrect. Adrenal insufficiency is not the mechanism.
Incorrect. The dual disturbance is the classic feature.
Incorrect. NHE3 inhibition is not the principal mechanism.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old researcher studies the buffering of an acid load in the body. After acute ingestion of a strong acid, which buffer system reacts FASTEST?
explanations: Incorrect. Bone is slow (hours-days for acute, weeks-months for chronic).

Correct. The bicarbonate buffer system responds within seconds to minutes. Cellular buffering (intracellular proteins, phosphates) follows over minutes to hours. Renal compensation (NH4+ excretion adaptation) takes days. Bone (chronic acid load) buffers over weeks-months but contributes significantly to chronic acidosis like CKD.
Incorrect. Renal compensation is slow (days).
Incorrect. Hepatic urea cycle is involved in nitrogen / ammonia handling, not acute acid buffering.
Incorrect. Erythropoiesis is unrelated.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old researcher studies how chronic acidosis affects ammoniagenesis. After 4 days of dietary acid loading, urinary NH4+ excretion has tripled. Which mechanism best explains this?
choices: Acidosis upregulates glutaminase and PEPCK in PCT
explanations: Correct. Chronic acidosis upregulates glutaminase (and PEPCK) in PCT cells, increasing ammoniagenesis. Each NH4+ excreted represents 'new' HCO3− added to plasma. The adaptation takes 3–5 days to develop and is the principal mechanism by which kidneys defend against chronic acid loads. CKD patients lose this capacity, contributing to chronic metabolic acidosis.
Incorrect. Tubular flow is not the principal driver.
Incorrect. Acidosis does not principally drive aldosterone (volume status does).
Incorrect. ADH is unrelated to NH4+ excretion.
Incorrect. AQP2 is for water, not NH4+.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old researcher studies aldosterone's effect on distal H+ secretion. Which mechanism explains how aldosterone enhances α-intercalated cell H+-ATPase activity?
choices: ENaC-driven lumen-negative voltage favors H+ extrusion
explanations: Incorrect. The effect is indirect via principal-cell-driven voltage.

Correct. Aldosterone drives ENaC-mediated Na+ reabsorption in adjacent principal cells, generating a lumen-NEGATIVE transepithelial voltage. This voltage favors H+ secretion at α-intercalated cells (and K+ secretion at principal cells). Aldosterone also directly stimulates the H+-ATPase in α-intercalated cells. Net effect: increased renal acid excretion. Hyperaldosteronism produces metabolic alkalosis; hypoaldosteronism produces hyperkalemic acidosis (type 4 RTA).
Incorrect. Aldosterone activates (not blocks) Na+/K+-ATPase in principal cells.
Incorrect. Pendrin is on β-intercalated cells (alkalosis defense).
Incorrect. Aldosterone does not principally stimulate CA.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old researcher studies how respiratory acidosis is renally compensated. After 4 days of CO2 retention from chronic respiratory disease, plasma HCO3− has risen from 24 to 36 mEq/L. Which mechanism produced this rise?
explanations: Correct. Chronic respiratory acidosis is renally compensated by increased H+ secretion and NH4+ excretion in the kidneys, with corresponding 'new' HCO3− addition to plasma. The full response takes 3–5 days. Expected: HCO3− rises by ~3.5 mEq/L per 10 mmHg PCO2 elevation in chronic compensation (vs ~1 in acute). Failure to compensate suggests superimposed metabolic acidosis.
Incorrect. Increased respiratory rate would lower CO2.
Incorrect. CO2 production is from metabolism, not the compensation route.
Incorrect. Aldosterone is not the principal mechanism.
Incorrect. GI HCO3− is minor.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old researcher studies respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis. Which best characterizes the expected respiratory compensation?
choices: PCO2 falls by 5 mm Hg per 1 unit pH drop
PCO2 rises proportionally to anion gap
explanations: Incorrect. PCO2 falls in metabolic acidosis (compensatory hyperventilation).

Correct. Winters formula: predicted PCO2 = 1.5 × [HCO3−] + 8 ± 2. If actual PCO2 is appropriately low per this formula → pure metabolic acidosis with appropriate compensation. Higher-than-predicted PCO2 → superimposed respiratory acidosis (mixed disorder). Lower-than-predicted PCO2 → superimposed respiratory alkalosis. Compensation begins within minutes; full effect within hours; PCO2 rarely falls below ~10 mmHg.
Incorrect. Not the standard compensation formula.
Incorrect. PCO2 changes with respiratory drive in metabolic acidosis.
Incorrect. The Winters formula uses HCO3−, not anion gap.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man has chronic kidney disease (eGFR 25) with metabolic acidosis (HCO3− 18). Which mechanism best explains the acidosis?
choices: Reduced ammoniagenesis from fewer functioning nephrons
explanations: Incorrect. Acute hyperkalemia is a separate phenomenon.

Correct. CKD-associated metabolic acidosis principally results from reduced renal ammoniagenesis (fewer functioning nephrons → less NH4+ excretion → reduced 'new' HCO3− regeneration). Phosphate retention contributes (less HPO4²− available as titratable acid). Bone buffering of chronic acidosis can lead to mineral loss / osteoporosis. Treatment: oral sodium bicarbonate or oral citrate to maintain HCO3− >22 — slows CKD progression and improves outcomes.
Incorrect. Bone calcium loss is a CONSEQUENCE of chronic acidosis, not the cause.
Incorrect. Respiratory rate often increases (compensation).
Incorrect. Gastric acid loss would cause alkalosis.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old researcher studies how the kidney generates 'new' bicarbonate to replace HCO3− consumed in buffering acid. Which process generates new HCO3−?
choices: Filtration of HCO3− at the glomerulus
PCT NHE3 H+ secretion (recycles existing HCO3−)
Each NH4+ excreted represents new HCO3− added to plasma
explanations: Incorrect. Filtration is the start of HCO3− handling but does not generate new HCO3−.
Incorrect. PCT NHE3 reabsorbs filtered HCO3− but does not generate new HCO3−.

Correct. Each NH4+ excreted in urine represents 'new' HCO3− added to plasma (because the H+ that joined NH3 to form NH4+ came from carbonic acid dissociation in the cell, and the matched HCO3− stays with the body). Same principle for titratable acid (each H+ secreted on phosphate generates an HCO3− retained). Net acid excretion (NH4+ + TA − HCO3− loss) ≈ daily acid load.
Incorrect. Tubular HCO3− secretion (β-intercalated cells) excretes excess HCO3−, not generates it.
Incorrect. Bone is not the principal renal mechanism.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old researcher studies the difference between α- and β-intercalated cells. Which best characterizes their relative roles?
choices: α: H+ secretion; β: HCO3− secretion
α: HCO3− secretion; β: H+ secretion
explanations: Incorrect. Only α-intercalated cells secrete H+; β secrete HCO3−.

Correct. α-intercalated cells: APICAL H+-ATPase + H+/K+-ATPase (acid-secreting); BASOLATERAL Cl−/HCO3− exchanger (AE1) returning HCO3− to plasma. β-intercalated cells: APICAL pendrin (Cl−/HCO3− exchanger, secreting HCO3−); BASOLATERAL H+-ATPase. The two cell types are functional mirror images, allowing the kidney to handle both acid and alkali loads. β-cells become more prominent in alkalosis.
Incorrect. Reversed roles.
Incorrect. Only β-cells secrete HCO3−.
Incorrect. They have opposite roles.
